answers.java_tx_design: I've worked on three separate modules of our tax platform over ten years: return intake, the assessment engine, and refund disbursement, and the clearest transaction-boundary problem came from the assessment engine. For a long time, validating a filed return, computing the assessed liability, and writing an audit-flag record all happened inside one transaction, because it felt safer to have everything succeed or fail together. Once we onboarded a large employer-withholding batch that submits about 80,000 returns overnight during the annual filing deadline, that combined transaction started holding row locks on the taxpayer_account table for 300-500ms each, because the audit-flag computation queried a slow-changing but large historical table. We measured over 400 blocked transactions during one overnight run, pushing total batch time from under an hour to nearly four hours, missing our processing window before the morning intake opened. I separated it: assessment and liability computation commit together, since those must be atomic for correctness, and the audit-flag check moved to an asynchronous step reading from a queue populated in the same transaction. Batch time returned to under an hour. The failure I hadn't anticipated: the audit queue's consumer wasn't sized for the new volume and fell behind by two days during the next peak, so I added a second consumer and an alert on queue age past four hours.
answers.java_ops: Operationally, the most significant problem I owned was JVM pause times on our refund-disbursement service during the two weeks each year when disbursement volume is highest. We were running the G1 collector with defaults, and once daily disbursement volume passed around 300,000 records, we saw GC pauses climbing from under 100ms to 900ms roughly every fifteen minutes, enough to trip our internal SLA of 200ms p99 for the disbursement-confirmation API that other government systems poll. I pulled GC logs and found allocation rate from building large in-memory batches of disbursement records before writing them was the driver, not an actual memory shortage. I changed the batch-write logic to stream disbursement records in chunks of 1,000 instead of assembling the full batch in memory first, which reduced allocation pressure substantially, and increased young-generation size proportionally on the smaller remaining allocation load. Pause frequency dropped to about once every ninety minutes, and pause length came down to under 150ms even during peak. It took two iterations: my first attempt only touched heap sizing without the streaming change, which reduced pause length somewhat but did nothing for frequency, since the underlying allocation pattern hadn't changed.
answers.rust_readiness: I do have production Rust experience. About four years ago I built and still maintain a refund-eligibility scoring service that flags claims likely to need manual fraud review before a refund is disbursed. We chose Rust because the scoring needs to run within a strict 15ms budget as part of the synchronous disbursement-approval path, and an earlier Java prototype of similar logic sat at 60-90ms at p99, largely due to GC pauses interrupting the scoring computation during the exact windows we couldn't tolerate delay. The Rust service uses tokio and communicates with the Java disbursement service over gRPC, returning a risk score and a set of contributing factors for any claim flagged for review. It currently processes around 150 requests per second at peak filing season, holding p99 under 10ms. The failure worth mentioning: about a year and a half in, a change to how we loaded a large reference table of known-risky bank routing numbers caused a startup delay that grew slowly as the table grew, eventually taking over two minutes and tripping our readiness-probe timeout during deploys; I found it profiling startup with perf and fixed it by loading the table lazily in the background instead of blocking readiness on it.
answers.rust_boundary: For the scoring service, I placed the boundary at the point right before a refund claim's disbursement approval: the Java disbursement service assembles the claim's features, calls the Rust service over gRPC, and only proceeds with disbursement once it has a decision back, whether that's an automatic approval or a flag for manual review. I kept the Rust service stateless with respect to the actual disbursement record itself, so a bug there can delay or flag a claim incorrectly but cannot corrupt disbursement data, which stays entirely on the Java side. Before migrating from the Java prototype, we measured its p99 latency and its correlation between GC pauses and scoring delay; after the Rust version shipped, we tracked p99, error rate, and ran both scorers side by side on a portion of real claims for about eight weeks, comparing their flag decisions before letting Rust's decision be authoritative. About 0.6% of claims disagreed during that period, traced to a difference in how the two implementations handled a specific missing-field case, which we fixed and re-verified before cutting over fully. For a ledger-style write path rather than a scoring sidecar, I would apply the same measured, shadow-run approach, but I would want a longer verification period given the higher cost of getting a write wrong.
answers.money_correctness: Every refund disbursement in our system carries an idempotency key composed of the claim ID and a disbursement attempt sequence number, enforced by a unique constraint on the disbursements table, so a retried request from our own retry logic after a timeout, or a resent request from a downstream banking integration, returns the existing disbursement record rather than issuing funds twice. This broke about three years ago: a banking partner's confirmation callback endpoint started timing out during a period of elevated load on their end, and our retry logic resent 64 disbursement requests over roughly six hours, but a bug in how the sequence number was generated caused it to reset to zero after a service restart mid-incident, so those 64 retries collided with existing sequence numbers and were silently treated as duplicates of unrelated, earlier claims. Twelve of those 64 were genuine new disbursements that got dropped entirely instead of processed, worth about $54,000 combined. I found this during weekly reconciliation against the banking partner's settlement file, which showed twelve claims marked approved in our system with no matching outbound payment. I corrected those twelve with new disbursement entries, not edits to the collided records, and fixed the sequence-number generator to persist its counter durably instead of resetting on restart.
answers.incident_response: Separately, we had an incident where the refund-eligibility scoring service, before the startup-delay fix I described, briefly returned a default 'low risk' score for every claim during a two-minute window right after a deploy, because the readiness probe passed before the risk-factor reference table had actually finished loading, so claims were scored against an effectively empty rule set. During that window, 47 claims were approved without the risk checks that would normally apply, three of which were later confirmed as fraudulent, totaling about $11,000. I noticed the anomaly the same day, from a routine check of score-distribution metrics that looked unusually uniform for that window, well before any of the three fraudulent claims had been reported externally. I scoped the affected 47 claims within about two hours by cross-referencing deploy timestamps against claim-approval timestamps, and referred all 47 for manual review immediately, not just the three later confirmed as fraudulent. I reported the gap to my lead and our fraud-operations team the same afternoon, before I had fully understood the root cause, since I thought people needed to know the window existed regardless of how it got fixed. The postmortem's lasting change was making the readiness probe actually depend on the reference table finishing its load.
answers.process_skipping: During that scoring-gap incident, once I understood the cause, I was tempted to push the readiness-probe fix straight to production without our normal review cycle, since I knew exactly what needed to change and wanted to close the window as fast as possible. What I actually did was resist that: I got a colleague to review the change over a short call, about fifteen minutes, rather than skipping review, explaining the urgency so they could focus their attention efficiently rather than treating it as routine. That review caught something I'd missed -- my first version of the fix would have blocked the readiness probe indefinitely if the reference table failed to load at all, rather than failing after a bounded timeout with an alert, which would have turned a scoring gap into a full outage under a different failure mode. I've never fully skipped a review step in ten years here; the closest I've come is compressing it under real time pressure the way I did in this case, always with the urgency stated up front rather than assumed, and always still getting at least one other set of eyes before deploying.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing a mistake: I once introduced a configuration change to the disbursement service's timeout settings that I believed was safe, and it was actually the underlying cause of the sequence-number collision I described in the money-correctness incident, since the shorter timeout increased how often retries fired under load. I found this myself while writing the postmortem, several days after the immediate incident had been resolved, and I updated the postmortem document to name my change as the contributing cause rather than leave the root cause as 'a service restart during elevated load,' even though nobody had specifically asked me to trace it that far back. On-call: I've carried on-call for the refund-disbursement and scoring services for about seven years, currently one week in five, and I handle escalations from our fraud-operations team directly rather than deferring them to someone else. I mentor one engineer currently, mostly by walking through incidents like these together afterward, and I genuinely think that kind of retrospective work has taught me more about the actual system than any of the original design work did.
answers.evidence_decision: About five years ago, the team debated whether to move refund-eligibility scoring off a simple Java rules engine onto a full machine-learning model, arguing it would catch more fraud patterns than hand-written rules could. I was skeptical of the model-based approach at the time and pulled six months of our own fraud-case data, showing that our existing rules engine was already catching about 91% of confirmed fraud cases, and that the model's projected improvement, based on a vendor's own benchmark, was uncertain enough given our comparatively small labeled dataset that I didn't trust the number. The team discussed my analysis and decided to hold off on a full model-based system, opting instead for the rules-engine-plus-Rust-performance-rewrite I eventually built, revisiting the model question once we had more labeled fraud data. I didn't quietly build a competing model in the meantime; three years later, once we had a much larger labeled dataset from operating the Rust scorer, I was the one who reopened the model conversation, since by then the data situation had genuinely changed and I thought it was worth revisiting rather than defending my earlier position out of habit.
answers.own_contribution: In the scoring-service work I described, the Rust implementation itself, the gRPC boundary design, the shadow-comparison period, and the startup-delay diagnosis and fix were all my own work. What the team contributed: our fraud-operations analysts define the actual risk factors and thresholds the service evaluates, which I implement but don't design myself, and two other engineers built the claim-feature-assembly code on the Java side that gathers the inputs the scoring service consumes. For the assessment-engine transaction-boundary redesign I described earlier, the diagnosis and the outbox-style redesign were mine, but a colleague implemented the second audit-queue consumer I mentioned adding later, from a short specification I wrote, since I was occupied with the scoring-service startup issue around the same time. I think naming that split matters, since 'I built the scoring service' and 'the team scaled the audit queue afterward' are genuinely different pieces of work, done by different people.
answers.java_recovery: The twelve dropped disbursements from the sequence-number collision are my clearest recovery example. I scoped it with a query joining disbursements against the banking partner's settlement export for the affected date range, looking for claims marked approved in our system with no matching outbound payment reference, which gave me the exact twelve out of the 64 retried requests. For each, I confirmed against the banking partner's own transaction log that no payment had actually gone out, rather than assuming every collision was a dropped payment, since some of the 64 were legitimate duplicate-suppression working correctly. I corrected the twelve with new disbursement entries carrying a corrected, durable sequence number, then manually re-ran our weekly reconciliation against just those twelve claim IDs afterward to confirm the banking partner's records matched ours. My first assumption, before checking carefully, was that all 64 retried requests had been affected; narrowing it to twelve required checking each one's sequence number against what it had actually collided with, since most of the 64 had simply been correctly suppressed as true duplicates.
answers.java_perf_change: Our claim-status lookup endpoint, used by taxpayers checking their refund status through the public portal, sat at p99 of 1.6 seconds during filing season against a target of 400ms. I measured with a profiler and found we were joining against a claim-history table for every lookup to support an audit-trail feature almost no taxpayer used from that particular screen, when only the current status was actually needed for the common case. My first attempt was adding a response cache with a short TTL, which helped average latency but did little for p99, since most lookups were for recently-filed claims that rarely repeated within the cache window. What worked was splitting the query so the common status-only path skipped the claim-history join entirely, which took p99 down to about 180ms, while keeping the full history available behind a separate, explicitly slower endpoint for the audit-trail feature so we weren't removing functionality, just not paying its cost on every request. I verified the change held up by comparing p99 across the following three filing seasons rather than declaring success after one clean measurement.
answers.rust_hands_on: In the scoring service, the ownership problem that took longest to resolve was around the risk-factor reference table itself: I wanted the background loader task to replace the whole table atomically once loaded, while request-handling tasks kept reading from whatever version was currently live, without blocking reads during the swap. My first attempt wrapped the table in a single Mutex, which technically worked but meant every scoring request briefly contended with the loader during a reload, adding latency spikes I couldn't afford in a 15ms budget. I moved to an Arc<RwLock<Table>>, wrapped further so the loader builds a completely new table off to the side and only takes the write lock briefly to swap the Arc, meaning readers never block on the actual loading work, only on the near-instant pointer swap. The Send/Sync issue came later, when I tried to share a metrics-reporting handle across tasks that wrapped a type from an early version of a logging library that wasn't Sync; the compiler correctly refused to compile it, and I eventually found the library exposed a Sync-safe cloneable handle under a name I hadn't noticed on first read of its documentation.
answers.rust_when_not: I would not move our claim-status lookup endpoint or most of the assessment engine's audit and reporting paths to Rust, even though the scoring service's success might make that tempting, because they change frequently as tax law and reporting requirements change each year, and the team maintaining them day to day is entirely Java-focused. A rewrite there would trade a measured performance problem we don't actually have for a maintenance burden the team isn't equipped to carry. I did hold back a real urge once: after the scoring service shipped successfully, I wanted to also rewrite our legacy penalty-calculation module, an older but still heavily used piece of code, in Rust largely because I'd enjoyed the scoring-service work. When I measured it honestly, its own p99 was 12ms against no real latency budget pressure at all, and its actual complexity was in tax-law-driven business rules that change with each legislative session, which our compliance team, not engineers, needs to be able to reason about directly in the code. I raised the idea, measured it, and dropped it once the numbers didn't support it, rather than building a case for it after the fact.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During a quarterly reconciliation about two years ago, our totals were short by about $6,300 across roughly 12,000 disbursements for the quarter, small individually but consistent enough that I wanted a real explanation rather than writing it off as rounding. I traced it to a batch of 19 claims where a taxpayer had filed an amended return after their original refund had already been disbursed, and our amendment logic recalculated the full refund amount and issued the difference as a second disbursement, but for those 19 cases a second amendment arrived before the first amendment's disbursement had settled with the banking partner, so the second amendment's calculation was based on a stale, not-yet-settled state. I corrected those nineteen with adjusting entries recalculated from the final settled state rather than the intermediate one, and added a check that blocks a new amendment's disbursement calculation from starting until the prior amendment's disbursement is confirmed settled. My first hypothesis was a currency-rounding accumulation issue, since $6,300 across 12,000 disbursements looked plausible for that, and I only found the real cause after checking each of the nineteen cases' amendment timelines individually against settlement timestamps.
answers.prod_data_verification: Yes, more than once. The clearest case was during the sequence-number collision incident, where I wanted to confirm which of the 64 retried requests were genuine drops versus correctly suppressed duplicates, and what I did was take that week's disbursement and settlement records, strip taxpayer names and account numbers, and run my comparison query against that masked copy in a separate database rather than live. For confirming the scoring service's startup-delay fix actually resolved the readiness-probe issue under real deploy conditions, I tested that by deliberately triggering several deploys in our staging environment configured to match production's reference-table size, rather than experimenting with deploy timing in production itself. The one time I checked a live figure directly was confirming the $54,000 total from the sequence-number incident for the postmortem, which I did with a read-only query, mentioned in our incident channel before running it, since I wanted an accurate number for the record rather than an estimate, not because I needed to verify anything was working.
